gutenberg.parties: Johann Fust, financier · against · Johannes Gutenberg, printer
body: Gutenberg did not lose his workshop to a rival or a fire. He lost it to his investor, in court, in the same year he finished the Bible.

Fust had lent him roughly 1,600 guilders across two loans to build the printing operation. When Fust called the debt in, Gutenberg could not pay, and the argument turned on what the money had been: a loan against the business, or a partnership investment that shared the risk. The surviving record of the judgment, the Helmasperger Notarial Instrument of November 1455, is the only near-contemporary document of the dispute, and it is written from Fust's side.

Fust won. He took the type, the presses, and the finished Bibles, and carried on printing with Peter Schöffer, who had been Gutenberg's own assistant and who later married Fust's daughter. The books that made the reputation went out under their names.

Gutenberg kept printing on a smaller scale and was eventually given a courtier's pension by the Archbishop of Mainz, which supplied clothing, grain and wine rather than money. He died in 1468 without ever being credited on a page he printed.
gutenberg.holding: The court ordered Gutenberg to repay the loans with interest, which transferred the working equipment to Fust.
gutenberg.legacy: The oldest founder-ousted-by-investor story in print, and the reason the first mass-produced European books carry Fust and Schöffer's imprint instead of Gutenberg's.

sources.title: Johannes Gutenberg: the lawsuit with Fust
Helmasperger Notarial Instrument

adele.court: Supreme Court of the United States, then binding arbitration in Austria
adele.parties: Maria Altmann, heir · against · the Republic of Austria
body: Adele Bloch-Bauer's portraits were taken from her family's Vienna apartment after the Anschluss in 1938. Austria hung the golden one in the Belvedere for the rest of the century and called it 'The Lady in Gold', which conveniently removed the Jewish family name from the most famous painting in the country.

Maria Altmann, Adele's niece, was in her eighties and living in Los Angeles when she tried to get them back. Austria's position was that a sovereign state cannot be sued in an American court, and that Adele's will had asked for the paintings to go to the national gallery. Altmann's lawyers pointed out that Adele never owned them: her husband Ferdinand did, and his will left everything to his nephews and nieces.

The Supreme Court question was narrow and procedural: does the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act of 1976 apply to things a foreign state did before 1976? On 7 June 2004 the Court said yes, which meant the case could proceed at all.

Austria then agreed to binding arbitration at home rather than fight in California. In January 2006 the panel ordered five of the six disputed Klimts returned. Adele Bloch-Bauer I sold to Ronald Lauder for a reported $135 million and hangs in the Neue Galerie in New York.
adele.holding: The Supreme Court held 6–3 that sovereign immunity under the FSIA applies retroactively, opening the courthouse door. The paintings themselves were won later, in arbitration.
adele.legacy: The precedent that lets private citizens sue foreign governments over Nazi-looted art, and the reason restitution claims still move paintings across borders today.

sources.title: Republic of Austria v. Altmann, 541 U.S. 677 (2004)
Six Klimt paintings: Maria Altmann and Austria

warhol-soup.court: Supreme Court of the United States
warhol-soup.parties: The Andy Warhol Foundation · against · Lynn Goldsmith, photographer
body: In 1981 Lynn Goldsmith photographed Prince for Newsweek. In 1984 Vanity Fair licensed one of her images as an 'artist reference' for a single illustration, paid her $400, and commissioned Warhol. Warhol made sixteen works from the photograph rather than one.

Nobody sued for decades. The fight started after Prince died in 2016, when the Warhol Foundation licensed 'Orange Prince' to Condé Nast for a commemorative magazine cover for $10,000 and Goldsmith received nothing and no credit. She raised her copyright; the Foundation sued first, seeking a declaration that the work was fair use.

The Court deliberately answered a small question. It did not rule on whether Warhol's silkscreens are art, whether he transformed the photograph, or whether making them was lawful. It looked only at the 2016 licensing, and asked what that specific use was for.

The answer was that both the photograph and the silkscreen were being used for the same thing, to illustrate a magazine story about Prince, and both were commercial. On that footing the first fair-use factor favoured Goldsmith. Justice Kagan's dissent, joined by the Chief Justice, argued the majority had flattened what artists actually do with source material.
warhol-soup.holding: Decided 7–2 on 18 May 2023. The first fair-use factor, purpose and character, favoured Goldsmith because the Foundation's commercial licensing shared the photograph's original purpose.
warhol-soup.legacy: The most consequential fair-use ruling in a generation for appropriation art, collage, sampling, and anyone training on or borrowing from copyrighted images.

sources.title: Opinion, No. 21-869 (PDF)
Case file and argument analysis
Supreme Court sides against the Warhol Foundation

hiphop.case: Grand Upright Music v. Warner Bros. Records
hiphop.court: U.S. District Court, Southern District of New York
hiphop.parties: Grand Upright Music, for Gilbert O'Sullivan · against · Biz Markie and Warner Bros.
body: Biz Markie built 'Alone Again' on a loop from Gilbert O'Sullivan's 1972 hit 'Alone Again (Naturally)'. His label had asked O'Sullivan for permission, been refused, and released the record anyway.

Judge Kevin Duffy opened his decision by quoting the seventh commandment: 'Thou shalt not steal.' He granted an injunction, ordered the album pulled, and referred the matter to prosecutors for possible criminal charges, which is not how commercial copyright disputes usually end.

Before this, sampling had operated on a practical assumption that small borrowings were part of the form and got sorted out afterwards, if at all. Records like Public Enemy's were built from dozens of uncleared fragments because clearing them was neither expected nor affordable.

Afterwards every sample had to be licensed in advance, which meant lawyers, budgets and refusals. Dense collage records became commercially impossible to make, and producers moved toward fewer, bigger, more expensive samples or replayed the parts themselves. The sound of the genre changed because of a ruling, not a trend.
hiphop.holding: Unlicensed sampling infringed the copyright in the sound recording. The court issued an injunction and referred the case for criminal investigation.
hiphop.legacy: The end of uncleared sampling. Sample clearance became an industry, and the collage-heavy sound of late-1980s hip-hop became legally unrepeatable.

sources.title: Grand Upright Music, Ltd. v. Warner Bros. Records, Inc.
How a 1991 ruling changed sampling

mcdonalds.case: McDonald's v. Steel and Morris (the McLibel case)
mcdonalds.court: High Court of Justice, England · then the European Court of Human Rights
mcdonalds.parties: McDonald's Corporation · against · Helen Steel and David Morris
body: Two London activists handed out a six-page pamphlet accusing McDonald's of, among other things, damaging the environment, exploiting children through advertising and paying poorly. McDonald's sued for libel.

English libel law at the time put the burden on the defendants to prove every claim true, and offered no legal aid for libel. Steel and Morris, an unwaged single mother and a part-time postal worker, represented themselves against a corporate legal team for 313 court days, which made it the longest trial in English legal history.

The judgment in June 1997 went mostly to McDonald's, with £60,000 in damages, later cut to £40,000 on appeal. But the judge also found several of the pamphlet's charges proven, including that McDonald's advertising exploited children and that the company paid low wages. The company never collected.

In February 2005 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that the UK had breached the defendants' right to a fair trial and to free expression by denying them legal aid in a case of that complexity. It awarded them damages against the British government.
mcdonalds.holding: McDonald's won the libel case but lost on several factual claims, and Britain was later found in breach of Articles 6 and 10 of the European Convention.
mcdonalds.legacy: The case that made 'McLibel' shorthand for corporations suing critics, drove reform of English libel law, and cost McDonald's far more in reputation than it recovered in damages.

sources.title: McLibel case
Steel and Morris v. United Kingdom

hot-sauce.case: Huy Fong Foods v. Underwood Ranches
hot-sauce.court: Ventura County Superior Court, California · affirmed by the Court of Appeal
hot-sauce.parties: Huy Fong Foods, maker of the rooster-bottle sriracha · and · Underwood Ranches, its grower
body: For 28 years one farm grew nearly all the red jalapeños in Huy Fong's sriracha. The arrangement ran on handshakes and annual agreements rather than a long-form contract, and Underwood Ranches restructured its entire operation around the one buyer.

The relationship collapsed in 2017 over money and acreage. Huy Fong sued first, claiming it had overpaid by about $1.5 million. Underwood counter-sued for breach and fraud, arguing it had planted and invested on assurances it would keep the business.

In July 2019 a jury sided with the farm: roughly $14.8 million in compensatory damages and $10 million in punitive damages, offset by the overpayment, for about $23.3 million net. The Court of Appeal affirmed the judgment in full in July 2021.

The hot sauce shortages that followed had other causes, chiefly drought and chili supply across Mexico and the American southwest, but the split removed the grower who had spent three decades breeding peppers specifically for that bottle.
hot-sauce.holding: The jury found Huy Fong liable for breach of contract and fraud, awarding Underwood Ranches about $23.3 million net. Affirmed on appeal in 2021.
hot-sauce.legacy: A reminder that an iconic consumer product can rest entirely on an undocumented handshake, and what it costs when that handshake fails.

sources.title: Sriracha maker loses lawsuit to its former jalapeño grower
Huy Fong ordered to pay millions to chili pepper supplier

origin.case: The State of Tennessee v. John Thomas Scopes
origin.court: Rhea County Circuit Court, Dayton, Tennessee
origin.parties: The State of Tennessee · against · John Scopes, substitute teacher
body: Tennessee's Butler Act made it unlawful to teach in a state-funded school any theory denying the biblical account of creation. Business leaders in the small town of Dayton saw a publicity opportunity, and recruited a 24-year-old substitute teacher to admit he had taught evolution so a test case could be staged there.

It worked beyond anyone's expectation. William Jennings Bryan, three-time presidential candidate, prosecuted. Clarence Darrow defended. It became the first American trial broadcast live on national radio, and reporters filed from a town that had gone looking for exactly this.

The trial's famous moment was not about Scopes at all. Darrow called Bryan himself as a witness on the Bible and questioned him on whether its days were literal days. The exchange was later struck from the record.

Scopes was convicted and fined $100. The Tennessee Supreme Court overturned the conviction in 1927 on a technicality, that the judge rather than the jury had set the fine, and pointedly declined to let the case go further. The Butler Act stayed law in Tennessee until 1967.
origin.holding: Convicted and fined $100. The conviction was reversed on a technicality in 1927, which denied both sides the constitutional ruling they wanted.
origin.legacy: The template for every courtroom fight over what schools may teach, and the reason Darwin's book still turns up in American legislative sessions a century later.

sources.title: Scopes Trial
The Scopes 'Monkey Trial' archive

balloon-dog.court: U.S. Court of Appeals, Second Circuit
balloon-dog.parties: Art Rogers, photographer · against · Jeff Koons
body: Art Rogers made a black-and-white photograph called 'Puppies': a couple on a bench holding a row of German shepherd puppies. It was licensed onto notecards, and Koons bought one.

Koons tore the copyright notice off the card, handed it to Italian artisans, and instructed them to copy it faithfully in painted wood, adding flowers in the hair. The result, 'String of Puppies', was made in an edition of three plus an artist's proof, and sold for a reported $367,000.

Koons argued parody and fair use: the sculpture was a comment on mass-produced sentimentality, and the banality of the source was the point. The court was unconvinced, noting that a parody must target the original work rather than society in general, and that nobody needed to see Rogers's photograph to get the joke.
The instructions to the artisans hurt him. Notes asking for the puppies to be copied 'as per photo' made it difficult to claim the source was incidental.
balloon-dog.holding: The Second Circuit affirmed that the sculpture infringed Rogers's copyright and rejected the fair-use defence.
balloon-dog.legacy: The case appropriation artists have argued with ever since, and a direct ancestor of the Warhol Foundation ruling three decades later.

sources.title: Rogers v. Koons
Case review: Rogers v. Koons

sherlock-holmes.case: Conan Doyle Estate v. Netflix (Enola Holmes)
sherlock-holmes.court: U.S. District Court, District of New Mexico · settled
sherlock-holmes.parties: The Conan Doyle Estate · against · Netflix, Legendary Pictures and author Nancy Springer
body: Almost every Sherlock Holmes story had already fallen into the American public domain. Ten late ones had not, so the estate's claim had to rest on something those ten stories uniquely contained.

Its argument was that in the final stories Conan Doyle gave Holmes warmth: he became capable of friendship, respect and feeling, partly written after the author lost his son in the First World War. Since the Enola Holmes film showed a Holmes with emotions, the estate argued, it was using protected material.

Courts had already been narrowing the estate's reach. In Klinger v. Conan Doyle Estate in 2014, the Seventh Circuit rejected the idea that a character stays under copyright until the last story does, with Judge Posner later calling the estate's licensing approach close to a shakedown.

The Enola Holmes case never produced a ruling. It was settled and dismissed in December 2020 on undisclosed terms, and the film had already been released. On 1 January 2023 the remaining stories entered the public domain and the question stopped mattering.
sherlock-holmes.holding: No decision. The case settled and was dismissed in 2020, and the underlying copyrights expired at the start of 2023.
sherlock-holmes.legacy: The high-water mark of arguing that a personality trait can be copyrighted, and a case study in using litigation as a licensing fee.

sources.title: Conan Doyle Estate Ltd. copyright disputes
Netflix sued over Sherlock Holmes' emotions

ysl.case: Comité Interprofessionnel du Vin de Champagne v. Yves Saint Laurent
ysl.court: Tribunal de grande instance de Paris, affirmed by the Paris Court of Appeal
ysl.parties: The Champagne growers' association · against · Yves Saint Laurent
body: In 1993 Yves Saint Laurent launched a perfume called Champagne, in a bottle shaped to echo a cork and a collar. The name was doing the obvious work: borrowing the associations of celebration and expense without selling any wine.

The Champagne region has spent more than a century building a legal wall around the word. Under French appellation law it is not a flavour or a style but a place, and producers outside the region cannot use it even on products that are unmistakably not wine.

The growers' association sued. On 28 October 1993 the Paris court invalidated the trademark and ordered the name off the product, and the Court of Appeal affirmed on 15 December. The reasoning ran on parasitism, a French doctrine covering the act of feeding off a reputation you did not build, rather than on any risk that shoppers would confuse a bottle of scent with a bottle of wine.
YSL kept the perfume and changed the name to Yvresse, a pun on ivresse, meaning intoxication. Bottles labelled Champagne became collectors' items precisely because they were withdrawn.
ysl.holding: The trademark was invalidated and the name prohibited in France on the basis of parasitism, not consumer confusion.
ysl.legacy: The clearest statement that an appellation is property, and the reason no European perfume, chocolate or candle is called Champagne today.

sources.title: Legal conflict over the protection of the designation Champagne
Yvresse (formerly Champagne)

yoga.case: Bikram's Yoga College of India v. Evolation Yoga
yoga.court: U.S. Court of Appeals, Ninth Circuit
yoga.parties: Bikram Choudhury · against · Evolation Yoga, founded by two of his former students
body: Bikram Choudhury's sequence is twenty-six postures and two breathing exercises, performed in a fixed order over ninety minutes in a room heated to about 105°F. He published it in a 1979 book, registered copyrights, and for years sent legal threats to studios teaching the same sequence under another name.
Evolation Yoga was founded by two people who had trained with him and who taught hot yoga using that sequence. Choudhury sued.

The Ninth Circuit ruled against him on 8 October 2015. Copyright protects expression, meaning the particular words and photographs in his book, but not the underlying idea, process or system those words describe. A sequence of poses intended to produce a health outcome is a system, and systems are for patents, which he did not have.

The court drew the comparison directly: a cookbook is copyrightable, the recipe it teaches is not; a surgical manual is protected, the operation is not. Choudhury's own framing of the sequence as a method that heals worked against him, because it argued the thing into the category copyright refuses.
yoga.holding: The sequence is an idea, process or system, not copyrightable expression. Choudhury lost.
yoga.legacy: The boundary line between a described method and the words describing it, applied to fitness, dance, cooking and every other physical practice sold as intellectual property.

sources.pub: U.S. Court of Appeals, Ninth Circuit
sources.title: Opinion, No. 13-55763 (PDF)
Bikram's Yoga College v. Evolation Yoga

barbie.case: Mattel and the Bild Lilli doll
barbie.court: U.S. District Court, then the Ninth Circuit
barbie.parties: Mattel · against, and sued by · Greiner & Hausser, makers of Bild Lilli
body: Barbie has a German predecessor. Lilli began as a comic-strip character drawn by Reinhard Beuthien for the tabloid Bild, and was made into a doll designed by Max Weissbrodt for the toy firm O&M Hausser, sold from 1955. She was an adult-figured novelty aimed at men, sold in bars and tobacconists rather than toy shops.
Ruth Handler encountered the doll on a European trip in 1956 and brought examples home. Barbie launched in 1959.

Litigation followed in March 1961, when Louis Marx and Company sued Mattel, alleging infringement of Greiner & Hausser's patent covering Lilli's hip joint and arguing Barbie was a direct copy. It did not succeed. In 1964 Mattel simply bought the problem: the Bild Lilli copyright plus German and US patent rights for three payments totalling 85,000 deutschmarks, roughly $21,600 at the time, with each side agreeing not to use the other's names. Lilli production stopped that year.

In 2001 Greiner & Hausser came back, arguing they had been pressured into that deal and seeking royalties on every Barbie sold since. The claim was dismissed, and the Ninth Circuit addressed the case in 2003.
barbie.holding: The 1961 suit failed; the 1964 purchase settled the rights for about $21,600; the 2001 attempt to reopen it was dismissed.
barbie.legacy: One of the best-documented cases of buying a predecessor rather than beating it, and the reason Barbie's origin story stayed quiet for forty years.

sources.title: Bild Lilli doll
Mattel, Inc. v. Greiner and Hausser GmbH (9th Cir. 2003)
Barbie's secret sister was a German novelty doll

rothko.court: New York County Surrogate's Court, affirmed by the Court of Appeals
rothko.parties: Kate Rothko and the estate · against · its own executors and the Marlborough Gallery
body: Rothko died in February 1970. Within three months his three executors sold 100 paintings to the Marlborough Gallery for $1.8 million payable over twelve years without interest, and consigned another 698 for sale at commissions up to fifty per cent.

Two of the executors had their own relationships with Marlborough. Bernard Reis was the gallery's accountant and an officer of it. Theodoros Stamos was a painter it represented, and shortly after the sale the gallery took him on. Rothko's daughter Kate, then in her twenties, sued to undo the whole arrangement.

The trial ran for years and turned on fiduciary duty rather than on art. On 18 December 1975 Surrogate Millard Midonick removed all three executors, voided the contracts, and held Reis, Stamos, the gallery and its owner Frank Lloyd jointly liable for $9,252,000, a figure driven by the market value of works already sold.
Marlborough was ordered to return 658 paintings that had not reached innocent buyers. Frank Lloyd was later convicted of tampering with evidence in the case.
rothko.holding: The executors breached their fiduciary duties through conflicts of interest. Contracts rescinded, executors removed, $9,252,000 in damages and fines assessed.
rothko.legacy: The case that rewrote how American courts police dealers, executors and artists' estates, and the reason conflict-of-interest rules in the art trade exist at all.

sources.title: Matter of Rothko, opinion archive
Art: Crushing Verdict (1975)

graffiti.court: U.S. District Court, Eastern District of New York, affirmed by the Second Circuit
graffiti.parties: 21 aerosol artists · against · developer Jerry Wolkoff and G&M Realty
body: 5Pointz was a Long Island City warehouse complex whose owner had let aerosol artists paint it for years, turning it into a destination that tour buses stopped at. When he moved to demolish it for luxury towers, the artists sued to save the work.

Their tool was the Visual Artists Rights Act of 1990, which gives artists limited moral rights in works of 'recognized stature', including the right not to have them destroyed. Nobody had seriously tested whether spray paint on someone else's wall qualified.

After the court declined an injunction but before demolition, Wolkoff had the building whitewashed overnight. Judge Frederic Block called it 'an act of pure pique and revenge for the nerve of the plaintiffs to sue', and noted he could have simply waited for his permits.
The court awarded the statutory maximum, $150,000 for each of 45 works, totalling $6.75 million. The Second Circuit affirmed in February 2020 and the Supreme Court declined to hear it that October.
graffiti.holding: Temporary graffiti can reach 'recognized stature' under VARA. The whitewashing was wilful, and the maximum statutory damages were upheld.
graffiti.legacy: Street art acquired enforceable legal standing, and property owners learned that permission to paint can become an obligation not to destroy.

sources.title: Developer who whitewashed 5Pointz owes artists $6.75m
Case review: Castillo et al. v. G&M Realty

statue-of-liberty.parties: Robert Davidson, sculptor · against · the United States Postal Service
body: In 2010 the Postal Service issued a Forever stamp showing the Statue of Liberty's face. It picked the image from a stock photo library and did not notice that the face was the wrong one.

The statue photographed stands outside the New York-New York casino in Las Vegas, sculpted by Robert Davidson in 1996. He had deliberately not copied Bartholdi exactly, giving her softer, more modern features, and had registered a copyright in his version.

The Postal Service printed about 4.9 billion of the stamps, earning roughly $2.1 billion in revenue and more than $70 million in profit, and kept selling them for months after the error came to light.

The court found Davidson's statue an original work rather than a slavish copy of a public-domain monument, and that the government's use was not covered by any statute. It awarded him $3,554,946.95 plus interest, a share of the profit the stamp had made.
statue-of-liberty.holding: Davidson's replica was independently copyrightable, and the Postal Service infringed it. Damages of about $3.55 million plus interest.
statue-of-liberty.legacy: A reminder that a copy can carry its own copyright if the copyist changed something, and the most expensive stock-photo mistake in postal history.

sources.title: Davidson v. United States, No. 13-942C (PDF)
Court orders USPS to put $3.5M check in the mail

polaroid.case: Polaroid Corp. v. Eastman Kodak Co.
polaroid.court: U.S. District Court, District of Massachusetts
body: Kodak had helped supply Polaroid with negative materials for years before deciding to enter instant photography itself in 1976. Polaroid sued within days.
In 1985 the court found Kodak had infringed seven of Polaroid's patents. An injunction in January 1986 forced it to stop making and selling instant cameras and film immediately.

About 16.5 million Kodak instant cameras had already been sold, and they became useless overnight once the film was withdrawn. Kodak ran an exchange programme offering owners a share, a disc camera or a bond, which cost it roughly half a billion dollars on its own.

Damages came in 1990. Polaroid had asked for around $12 billion. The court awarded about $909 million, made up of roughly $454 million in damages and $455 million in interest, at the time the largest patent judgment ever paid in the United States.
polaroid.holding: Kodak infringed seven Polaroid patents, was enjoined from the market in 1986, and paid about $909 million in 1990.
polaroid.legacy: The case that removed a giant from an entire product category, and the reason instant film remained Polaroid's alone until the patents aged out.

sources.title: Judge orders Kodak to pay $909 million
Polaroid v. Kodak, still the champ

birkin-bag.court: U.S. District Court, Southern District of New York
body: In December 2021 Mason Rothschild released 100 NFTs called MetaBirkins, each a digital image of a Birkin bag rendered in coloured fur. They sold briskly while NFT prices were peaking.

His defence was that they were artworks commenting on fashion, fur and value, and therefore protected speech, in the tradition of Warhol painting soup cans. Hermès argued this was a trademark being used to sell a product, and pointed to press coverage that described the project as a business.

The jury sided with Hermès on 8 February 2023, finding trademark infringement, dilution and cybersquatting, and awarding $110,000 plus $23,000, about $133,000 in total. The judge later ordered the domain and any future revenue handed over.
The damages were small; the precedent was not. It was the first trial to test whether First Amendment protection for artistic work extends to trademarks used inside digital goods.
birkin-bag.holding: The jury found the MetaBirkins likely to confuse consumers and not shielded by the First Amendment. Total damages about $133,000.
birkin-bag.legacy: The first American verdict on trademarks in NFTs, and the case every digital artist borrowing a logo now has to argue around.

sources.title: Hermès gets win over MetaBirkins in first NFT trademark trial
Case review: Hermès International v. Rothschild

ipod.court: Settled before trial, U.S. District Court and the ITC
ipod.parties: Creative Technology, maker of the Zen player · against · Apple
body: Creative had shipped hard-drive music players before the iPod and held a patent, granted in 2005, on a specific idea: navigating a music library through a hierarchy of screens, artist to album to track.

That is exactly how the iPod's click wheel worked. Creative sued in May 2006 and filed with the International Trade Commission, which could have blocked iPod imports into the United States entirely. Apple counter-sued.

Apple settled in August 2006, paying Creative $100 million for a paid-up licence covering all its products, with a clause letting it recoup part of the money if Creative licensed the patent to others.

Creative won the money and lost the market. It joined Apple's accessory programme and made iPod peripherals, having established that it invented the interface and that this was worth roughly one per cent of what the iPod earned.
ipod.holding: Settled. Apple paid $100 million for a licence to Creative's navigation patent, ending all suits between them.
ipod.legacy: A clean illustration that being first to an idea and winning the market are different contests, decided in different rooms.

sources.title: Apple and Creative announce broad settlement
Apple settles Creative lawsuits for $100M

sagrada-familia.case: Barcelona City Council and the Sagrada Família
sagrada-familia.court: Negotiated with the city, no trial
sagrada-familia.parties: Barcelona City Council · and · the Sagrada Família building board
body: Construction began in 1882. In 1885 the board applied to the town of Sant Martí de Provençals for a building licence. No answer ever came, Sant Martí was absorbed into Barcelona in 1897, and the paperwork was forgotten while the most visited monument in the city went up around it.

That made the basilica, for 137 years, an unlicensed building site. The point only became pressing as construction accelerated toward the 2026 completion target and the surrounding streets filled with tourists.

Rather than litigate, the two sides negotiated. In October 2018 the board agreed to pay the city €36 million over ten years toward public transport and street improvements around the site, covering the burden of decades of building.
The permit was finally issued in June 2019, valid to 2026, with a further fee of about €4.6 million. Barcelona's deputy mayor called the absence of a licence 'a historical anomaly'.
sagrada-familia.holding: No court ruling. A negotiated settlement of €36 million plus fees, and a building permit granted in June 2019.
sagrada-familia.legacy: Proof that planning law is enforced by attention rather than by time, and the rare case where a century of non-compliance ended in a cheque instead of a demolition order.

sources.title: Sagrada Família finally gets building permit after 137 years
Basilica to pay city €36 million in late permit fees

banksy.case: Full Colour Black v. Pest Control Office (the Flower Thrower mark)
banksy.court: EU Intellectual Property Office, Cancellation Division
banksy.parties: Full Colour Black, a greetings card company · against · Pest Control, Banksy's authentication body
body: Banksy's position on copyright was a published joke: 'Copyright is for losers.' Anonymity made enforcing it awkward anyway, since claiming a work means identifying yourself as its author.
Pest Control tried a workaround, registering the Flower Thrower image as an EU trade mark in 2014. Trade marks do not require you to reveal who you are, only that you use the mark in trade.

A greetings card company that had been selling Banksy images applied to cancel it. In response Banksy opened a shop in Croydon called Gross Domestic Product, displaying goods behind glass that customers could not buy, and said aloud that the point was to satisfy trade-mark law. That statement became evidence.

On 14 September 2020 the EUIPO cancelled the mark for bad faith, finding the shop was not genuine commercial use but an attempt to circumvent the law. The examiners noted the irony that the same image appears on the cover of a book in which Banksy praises disobeying copyright.
banksy.holding: The trade mark was declared invalid for bad faith, because the use shown was staged to satisfy the registration rather than to trade.
banksy.legacy: The clearest ruling yet that anonymity has a price in intellectual property, and that saying why you are doing something can be the thing that defeats you.

sources.title: Banksy loses trademark battle over Flower Thrower
Flower Thrower trade mark cancelled for bad faith

super-mario.court: U.S. Court of Appeals, Second Circuit
body: Donkey Kong was a hit in 1981, and it featured a large ape, a captured woman and a man climbing girders. Universal, which had made King Kong films, told Nintendo's licensees they were infringing and collected settlements from several of them.
Nintendo refused. Universal sued, and the case was handled for Nintendo by Howard Lincoln and an outside lawyer, John Kirby, whose name a later Nintendo character is often said to honour.

Nintendo's defence went at the root of the claim: Universal had itself argued in earlier litigation that the King Kong story was in the public domain, and had won on that basis. The court agreed there was no likelihood of confusion, and found Universal's chain of trademark rights defective.

The Second Circuit affirmed in 1984. Universal had sued over property it had previously told a court it did not exclusively own, and the district court found the claim brought in bad faith to take a share of Donkey Kong's profits.
super-mario.holding: Universal lost entirely. No likelihood of confusion, no valid trademark rights, and a finding that the claim was brought in bad faith.
super-mario.legacy: The case that kept Nintendo independent early enough to matter, funded by a company that tried to tax it.

sources.title: Universal City Studios v. Nintendo, 746 F.2d 112 (2d Cir. 1984)
Universal City Studios v. Nintendo, 615 F. Supp. 838 (S.D.N.Y. 1985)

monopoly.case: Anti-Monopoly, Inc. v. General Mills Fun Group
monopoly.court: U.S. Court of Appeals, Ninth Circuit
monopoly.parties: Ralph Anspach, economics professor · against · the owners of Monopoly
body: Ralph Anspach designed a game called Anti-Monopoly, in which players broke up trusts. Parker Brothers' owners threatened him, and rather than fold he sued to have the Monopoly trademark cancelled as generic.

Researching his defence, he uncovered the history the company had buried: the game descended from The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 by Elizabeth Magie, a Georgist who designed it to demonstrate how land monopoly impoverishes tenants. It had circulated for decades in homemade versions before Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935.

The Ninth Circuit held that Parker Brothers had promoted 'Monopoly' so successfully as the name of the game itself that consumers used it generically, and a generic term cannot be a trademark. Anspach won.
Then Congress amended the Lanham Act to overrule the reasoning, changing how genericness is tested. Monopoly's trademark survived by statute after losing in court.
monopoly.holding: The Ninth Circuit found the mark generic. Congress then amended trademark law to reverse the test the court had used.
monopoly.legacy: The lawsuit that recovered Elizabeth Magie from obscurity, and a rare case of a company losing in court and winning in the legislature.

dracula.parties: Florence Stoker, Bram Stoker's widow · against · Prana Film
body: Prana Film made Nosferatu in 1922 without buying the rights to Dracula. It changed the names, moved the setting and turned the count into Orlok, then advertised the film as freely adapted from Stoker's novel, which rather undercut the disguise.

Florence Stoker was living on her husband's royalties. She joined the British Incorporated Society of Authors and pursued Prana through the German courts for three years. Prana went bankrupt almost immediately, leaving her fighting a company with nothing to pay her.
In July 1925 the court ordered every copy of the film destroyed. She spent years afterwards chasing prints that surfaced in other countries and demanding they be burned, which very nearly worked.

Enough copies survived abroad for the film to be reconstructed. Dracula entered the public domain in the United States decades later, and Nosferatu is now considered among the most influential films ever made, which is to say it survived a court order sentencing it to death.
dracula.holding: The film infringed the novel's copyright. The court ordered all copies and negatives destroyed.
dracula.legacy: The most nearly successful attempt to erase a film from history, and the reason every vampire since owes something to a copy that escaped.

ulysses.case: United States v. One Book Called Ulysses
ulysses.court: U.S. District Court, Southern District of New York
ulysses.parties: The United States government · against · a book
body: American customs seized Ulysses as obscene, and under forfeiture procedure the case was brought against the object itself rather than against a person, which is why the defendant in the caption is a book.

Random House engineered the prosecution deliberately. It imported a copy, made sure customs noticed, and glued reviews and criticism into the volume so the court would have to consider the book's reputation as part of the evidence.

Judge John Woolsey read the whole novel. His December 1933 opinion held that the test was the effect of the book taken as a whole on a person of average sensibility, not the effect of isolated passages on the most susceptible reader. He found Ulysses difficult but not pornographic, describing its effect as 'somewhat emetic, nowhere does it tend to be an aphrodisiac'.
The Second Circuit affirmed in 1934. Random House published it in America the following month, and printed Woolsey's opinion in the front of the book, where many editions still carry it.
ulysses.holding: The novel was not obscene. Obscenity must be judged by the work as a whole and its effect on an average reader.
ulysses.legacy: The end of judging books by their dirtiest sentence, and the foundation of modern American obscenity law.

banned-books.case: Board of Education, Island Trees School District v. Pico
banned-books.court: Supreme Court of the United States
banned-books.parties: Steven Pico, a high-school student · against · his school board
body: A New York school board removed nine books from its libraries after board members attended a conservative conference and returned with a list. Among them were Slaughterhouse-Five, Black Boy and Soul on Ice. The board called them 'anti-American, anti-Christian, anti-Semitic, and just plain filthy'.
Steven Pico, then a student, sued with four classmates. The case ran for years and reached the Supreme Court while he was in college.

The Court splintered badly. No opinion commanded a majority, but a plurality held in 1982 that while boards have wide discretion over curriculum, they may not remove books from a library simply because they dislike the ideas in them.

Because it was a plurality, the precedent is weaker than its fame suggests, and it applies to removing books rather than to choosing which to buy. It remains the case both sides cite in every American library fight.
banned-books.holding: A plurality held that removing library books to suppress ideas violates the First Amendment, though school boards retain broad curricular discretion.
banned-books.legacy: The constitutional floor under every school-library dispute since, and the reason removals now get framed as selection decisions.

orwell-1984.court: U.S. District Court, Western District of Washington, settled
orwell-1984.parties: Justin Gawronski, a high-school student · against · Amazon
body: In July 2009 Amazon discovered that a publisher had uploaded editions of Nineteen Eighty-Four and Animal Farm to the Kindle store without holding US rights. It removed them, and also deleted the copies people had already bought, refunding the purchase price.

Customers woke to find the books gone from devices they owned. The title being retroactively unpublished from private libraries by a central authority was Nineteen Eighty-Four, which is the sort of coincidence no novelist would risk.
Justin Gawronski had been annotating the book for a school assignment and lost his notes along with the text. He sued, arguing Amazon's own terms promised customers a permanent copy.

Amazon settled, offering to restore the books or pay $30, and Jeff Bezos publicly called the deletion 'stupid, thoughtless, and painfully out of line with our principles'. Amazon changed its policy to stop deleting purchased books except under court order.
orwell-1984.holding: Settled, with Amazon restoring the books or paying $30 and changing its deletion policy.
orwell-1984.legacy: The clearest demonstration that a digital purchase is a licence someone else can revoke, taught using the one book guaranteed to make the point.

napster.court: U.S. Court of Appeals, Ninth Circuit
napster.parties: The major record labels and Metallica · against · Napster
body: Napster let users share MP3s directly with each other, but kept a central index of who had what. At its peak it had tens of millions of users and the industry had no legal way to sell them a single track.

Napster's defence leaned on the 1984 Betamax ruling, which protected the video recorder because it had substantial non-infringing uses. The Ninth Circuit distinguished it: Napster's central index meant the company knew what was being traded and could have stopped it.

That knowledge and control was fatal. The court affirmed an injunction in February 2001 requiring Napster to police its own network, which it could not do at scale, and the service shut down that July.
The ruling pushed file sharing toward genuinely decentralised networks with no index to seize, which proved harder to sue. The labels won the case and spent the next decade losing the format.
napster.holding: Napster was liable for contributory and vicarious infringement because it knew of and could control the infringing traffic.
napster.legacy: The end of the first file-sharing era and the direct cause of both decentralised piracy and, eventually, licensed streaming.

google.court: Supreme Court of the United States
body: Google built Android using roughly 11,500 lines of Java API declaring code, the names and structures programmers use to call functions, so that Java developers could write for Android without learning a new vocabulary. It wrote its own implementations underneath.

Oracle bought Sun, which had made Java, and sued for about $9 billion. The case ran for a decade through two jury trials and multiple appeals, with the Federal Circuit twice reversing findings in Google's favour.

In April 2021 the Supreme Court ruled 6–2 for Google. It assumed without deciding that the declaring code could be copyrighted, then held that copying it to let programmers use their existing skills on a new platform was fair use.

Justice Breyer compared the API to the layout of a typewriter keyboard or a filing system: valuable largely because people have learned it, so locking it up would let one company charge rent on other people's training.
google.holding: Decided 6–2. Copying the Java API declaring code to build a new platform was fair use. The Court left the copyrightability question open.
google.legacy: The ruling that kept software interfaces broadly reusable, and the reason competitors can still build compatible systems without a licence.

tetris.court: U.S. District Court, District of New Jersey
tetris.parties: Tetris Holding · against · Xio Interactive, maker of Mino
body: Xio did its homework before building its game. It read the case law, understood that game rules and mechanics cannot be copyrighted, and set out to copy only the unprotectable parts of Tetris.

It copied more than that. Mino used the same playfield dimensions, the same seven piece shapes in the same colours, the same shadow showing where a piece would land, the same display of the next piece. Xio admitted the copying and argued every element was dictated by the rules.

The court disagreed. Rules can be expressed in countless ways, and Xio had reproduced the specific expressive choices rather than the underlying system. Its own care became evidence, since its research showed the copying was deliberate and precise.
The ruling drew the line where video game cloning lives: you may build a falling-block puzzle, but not one that looks like someone else's falling-block puzzle.
tetris.holding: Copying Tetris's visual expression infringed, even though the game's rules and mechanics were free to use.
tetris.legacy: The most cited authority on game clones, and the reason imitators change the palette and proportions rather than the mechanics.

mona-lisa.parties: The Italian state · against · Vincenzo Peruggia, glazier
body: Peruggia had worked at the Louvre fitting protective glass. In August 1911 he hid overnight, walked out with the Mona Lisa under his smock, and kept her in a trunk in his Paris room for two years while France searched and the press made her famous.

He was caught in 1913 trying to sell her to a Florence dealer, who alerted the authorities. Peruggia's defence was patriotic: he said he was returning a stolen Italian treasure to Italy, believing Napoleon had looted it.

That was wrong. Leonardo took the painting to France himself and it was bought by François I. But the story landed in an Italy receptive to it, and he was treated in much of the press as something close to a hero.

The court convicted him and gave him a sentence of about a year, reduced on appeal to roughly seven months, and he served little of it. Italy exhibited the painting around the country before returning it to the Louvre.
mona-lisa.holding: Convicted of theft. The sentence was reduced on appeal to a matter of months.
mona-lisa.legacy: The theft that made the Mona Lisa the most famous painting in the world, punished as though it had been a minor act of patriotism.
